Mr. Speaker, the last speaker, the former premier of New Brunswick, could not have confirmed more adequately the belief held by a number of people in this party that the heart and core of the thinking of the Conservative party is essentially the same as the heart and core of the economic thinking of the present government. I say this, of course, without suggesting any disrespect for the seriousness and earnestness with which opinions are held by the hon. member, but simply to make a philosophical point that for many people Adam Smith died in the eighteenth century, but for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) and for the spokesman for the Conservative party who has just sat down, it is evidently clear that Adam Smith is reigning supreme.
If you just look at the bill that is before us, Bill C-201, and consider the objections that have been brought against the motion introduced by the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman), it is clear that for example, the minister's thinking in economic matters was warped and perverted by his early liberalism, at the University of Ottawa presumably, where it was drummed into his head that there was a radical and profound distinction to be made between economic matters on the one hand and political matters on the other, and never the twain shall meet. He is like Thomas Hobbes, seventeenth century theorist; me, more like John Locke who was somewhat of a Democrat. At the same time he has the eighteenth century view of economics held by Adam Smith, which is also found in the thinking of Hobbes and Locke in any case. They made the same distinction 200 years ago that we heard in the hon. member's speech and that is the guts of this bill, between economic, social and political matters, the view of social reality that the more progressive and imaginative intellectual spheres began to disregard in the latter eighteenth, nineteenth and twentieth centuries. One would have hoped that that kind of distinction would have been irrevocably shattered, but alas it still resides very profoundly in the hearts of our cabinet members and, as I said, in the hearts of members of the Official Opposition.
Let us just look at the categories of the bill ostensibly designed to deal with the serious question of foreign ownership. If you look at the criteria that are to be considered in clause 2(2), paragraphs (a) to (e), you see references to economic activity in paragraph (a), to Canadians in the business enterprise in paragraph (b), to productivity, industrial efficiency and technological development in paragraph (c), to competition in paragraph (d) and to economic policies in paragraph (e). There is absolutely no reference to the impact on the lives of Canadians of economic decisions in terms of social and political reality. Surely, that is what society is all about. Surely, this is or should be a fundamental criterion in assessing the worth of the newly defined economic policy. It is not just a

matter of economic efficiency, of technological innovation and of competition but, much more significantly, of the effects on the political and social aspects of Canada, the degree to which it encourages or discourages independence in the broader sense of that word, not just economic independence but the extent to which a move may involve important questions of the political durability of Canada as a union linking one part with the other.
Let us consider, for example, the decision to establish Air Canada, originally Trans Canada Airlines. Was that just an economic decision? Surely not, or the economic thinking of the government of the day, which still exists, would not lead it to come up with the decision to have a publicly owned airline. There are, in short, profoundly important political considerations that must play a role in any decision making in this area, and they are just the kinds of considerations that the government is not interested in including in the heart of its bill.
It is very interesting that in the most recent issue of the Financial Times-and I cannot forbear the pleasure of mentioning this-the issue of June 26, at pages 15 and 16 there are two separate news items. The first one refers to the government's policy on the takeover bill. The heading reads "Softening the Takeover Act" and the opening paragraph reads:
The government has moved to meet business criticism of its takeover legislation. Industry Minister Pepin last week proposed four amendments to the Foreign Takeovers Review Act.
Then, it goes on to describe the amendments. It points out that each amendment is designed to please the corporate sector in Canada, that corporate sector which is overwhelmingly foreign owned. Readers of the Financial Times, most of whom would be supporters of the present corporate sector, would read that item with a great deal of pleasure.
Then, when they turn to page 16 they see another news item headed, "Ontario's Canadian Director Policy: Symbol, Not Threat." The opening paragraph in reference to the Ontario government's profoundly militant, profoundly imaginative, profoundly innovative action when it announced it was going to Canadianize Ontario industry by putting a few Canadians on boards of directors, reads-and the Financial Times, even though it is a conservative publication is interested in reality and not sham:
Ontario's plan to force all provincial companies to have a majority of Canadian citizens on their boards by October 1, 1973 only sounds tough.
The article goes on to conclude that that bit of action proposed by the Ontario government is all form, and is totally lacking in substance. It points out:
Business generally has reacted to the legislation nonchalantly.
In other words, the business community recognizes that kind of legislation for what it is. It serves to defuse the problem of getting real autonomy in Canadian economic matters by suggesting that a few more Canadians on boards will shift the direction of policy decisions. If there were real heart to that legislation, it would require effective guideline regulations and the imposition of sanctions, making it mandatory that Canadians on corporation boards must make decisions that have a positive influence

on research and development, on unemployment, on effective development of Canadian resources. That kind of substance is totally lacking in the Ontario legislation.
I just mention this to show that on two pages back to back in the Financial Times we have criticism of the Liberal government in Ottawa and of the Conservative government in Toronto. Here, in this chamber, we have had back to back speakers who, in philosophical outlook on economic matters, are absolutely in accord with the government, absolutely in agreement that the political state should not involve itself directly in influencing decisions by corporations that have an effect on the political and social affairs of Canada. It is a very revealing exercise.
Through our amendments we would make it mandatory on the government to ask such political questions as: what about the extraterritoriality question concerning foreign owned corporations? Will they obey United States law in terms of those to whom they may or may not sell goods? Will they be able to sell automobiles to China or the Soviet Union? Will they be able to hire foreign owned ships to transport wheat to China if this is contrary to the wishes of the United States government? This extraterritoriality question is profoundly important in terms of political significance, in terms of our being able to assess whether or not we are an independent nation.
The government would be able to intervene directly in terms of research and development matters which do not have just an economic impact. It could happen that a firm coming into Canada, which normally does a lot of research and development elsewhere, would provide a certain number of jobs and thus meet the narrowly defined economic criteria in the bill, but would do nothing to develop Canadian research and development potential, would do nothing to employ young Canadian scientists. Letting such a firm come into Canada without a research and development commitment, or allowing a takeover without insisting on a research and development department, would meet the narrow economic criteria but would not meet the political and social criteria. Our young people want to work in industry, and for the sake of the long-term economic interests of the country we must have a strong research and development industry.
The minister knows very well that the OECD report issued last fall, outlining a study of the ten leading industrial nations, put Canada far at the bottom of the list in terms of doing its own research and development. It was not just one step below the ninth on the list, but quite a way below it. To have a modern economy that will thrive and grow, we must have this kind of potential.
Some consideration must be given to the allocation of investment funds. Some consideration must be given to restriction of the Canadian banking industry. Is it going to be allowed to finance further takeovers? Is it going to be restricted to the financing of Canadian owned enterprises? There is nothing in this bill which says anything about that. There is nothing in this bill which deals with the existing levels of foreign ownership. Its provisions are all concerned with the future. It does nothing about the fact that 50 per cent of our manufacturing industry is foreign owned, 65 per cent of our mining and smelting industry is foreign owned, and 74 per cent of our
Foreign Takeovers Review Act petroleum and natural gas industry is foreign owned. All the government is concerned about is future takeovers, and this in a narrowly defined economic sense.
I could go on at length to list about 15 other things that the bill does not include that were mentioned in the committee and that were dismissed without serious argument by the minister. But I will not do so. I end up urging acceptance of our amendments, urging rejection of that narrow 18th century economic philosophy which separates economic from political and social considerations, and hoping that the House will support us.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak briefly on the amendment to Bill C-201 before the House. This bill is the government's answer to the foreign ownership crisis facing the Canadian nation. If ever a piece of legislation needed amendment, it is the one we are debating this afternoon. I feel this is an anaemic approach to the problem of foreign ownership in Canada. As we look over the record of this government, however, we must realize that it is a typical Liberal approach: Do nothing by halves if you can do it by quarters. This is exactly the position this government has taken, not only on the matter of foreign ownership but on other very important issues. I find it particularly disappointing.
Having been in this House for the past four years and having seen the amount of research and effort that has gone into the problem of foreign ownership from all sides of the House, I feel there is genuine desire on the part of Canadians to make sure that we have control of our destiny, that we have control of our resources. I feel that we do not have that control largely because governments in the past have not dealt with the problem effectively. It has been a bitter disappointment to Canadians to realize that the announced policy has nothing to do with the expansion of existing foreign-owned firms into new areas and new industries, which is one of the key problems facing us. It has nothing to do with direct foreign investment coming into Canada, and it does nothing to increase Canadian ownership in the areas with which we are directly concerned. It will not reduce the percentage of foreign control which presently exists in Canada: in fact, there is every indication that the opposite will be the result.
If I may go back to the amendment presently before the House, I should like to read the first portion of the clause because I think it should appear in Hansard to show what the government is offering and what our amendment will do. Clause 2(1) reads as follows:
This act is enacted by the Parliament of Canada in recognition by Parliament that the extent to which control of Canadian industry, trade and commerce has become acquired by persons other than Canadians and the effect thereof on the ability of Canadians to maintain effective control over their economic environment is a matter of national concern, and that it is therefore expedient to establish a means by which measures may be taken under the authority of Parliament to ensure that, in so far as is practicable after the enactment of this act, control of Canadian business enterprises may be acquired by persons other than Canadians only if it has been assessed that the acquisition of such control by those persons is or is likely to be of significant benefit to Canada,

One thousand vehicles would have been produced in a Canadian factory, by Canadian workers using Canadian raw materials. But what happened? No other country in the world should be able to tell us with whom we may trade. If we have an opportunity to sell goods to China, Cuba or any country in the world with whom we have friendly relations, the decision must rest with the Canadian people and not with some company in another part of the world.
The minister says we do not need this amendment. Mr. Speaker, other examples of interference were given to the House this morning when there was mention of a wheat sale. Apparently, because certain flour mills were under the control of United States companies, they were forbidden to ship flour to Cuba although the sale had initially been made to Russia. This is sheer and utter nonsense. We must be masters in our own house, but the bill before us does not give us that opportunity.
We hear about the effect and influence of foreign-owned companies on what is happening in Canada. Not long ago a conference on the environment was held in Stockholm. A strong delegation was sent from Canada; it offered to contribute $1 million toward global research into energy sources which would not create pollution, then suddenly the offer was dropped. The international press suggested that tremendous pressure had been put on the Canadian

delegation by the big oil companies. The fund was to be established to search for another source of energy which would not pollute to the degree that oil does. This is sound and sensible, yet Canada withdrew the offer of $1 million toward the $4 million fund.
All we have to do is look around the northern parts of Canada. Look at what is happening in Arctic exploration. Foreign corporations, by applying pressure to various departments of government, have forced them to water down the strictness of land use regulations affecting the Arctic and now the fragile economy of the area will not be protected to the extent that it should.
The minister knows this, yet he sits there and tries to appease the Canadian people by telling them that such activities have little effect on the social and political life of this nation. That is utter nonsense. If the minister thinks for one moment that he has sold this watered-down policy to the Canadian people, he had better think again. Young people especially, who want to enter the Canadian labour force but cannot find jobs, are concerned. Young people with university degrees cannot find work, partly as a result of foreign ownership policies the Liberal government has fostered over the years.
We are shipping out raw materials at an alarming rate. Insufficient quantities of raw materials are fabricated into products within the borders of Canada. The result is lack of jobs for Canadians in Canada. That is why we demand action to be taken. We are in favour of a screening process, which is all this bill deals with; we are in favour of screening takeovers. At the same time we ask the government to move into other fields of foreign ownership so that we may become masters in our own house.
That is why we urge the minister to accept our amendments. They will be of benefit. They will enable the government to screen on a basis other than that of straight economic policy. The minister cannot deny that. There is need for our amendments, I submit. For that reason we ask the minister to reconsider his position, to accept the amendment before us and to take a small step forward in adopting a tougher policy toward foreign ownership in Canada.

speechtext: I think the hon. member is getting too excited.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO CONTROL FOREIGN TAKEOVERS OF CANADIAN COMPANIES
speechtext:
The minister suggests that the control of our economic environment is sufficient, and that this matter comes first. I submit that the effects on our social and political environment flow directly from what happens in our economy. No doubt this has been the case throughout our history; that is the whole problem.
The amendment is an attempt to persuade the minister to at least help solve the problem by getting rid of that outmoded concept. The effects on the social and political environment should be given at least equal, if not greater,
3506

June 26, 1972
Foreign Takeovers Review Act consideration as the effects on the economic environment. These amendments Eire an attempt to get the minister to face up to that fact and recognize that the social and political environment is at least as important as the economic environment in the whole area of takeovers.
A company trying to accomplish a takeover should have to gUEirantee that certain social and political conditions will be met. If they cannot do that in addition to meeting the economic environment conditions, the takeover should not be allowed. Let me illustrate what I mean. If this amendment is accepted, and if a company in any industry contemplating a takeover cannot guarantee that its operations will not be affected by United States law or the law of any other country, the takeover should not be Eillowed. That has to do with the Canadian political environment. Surely the minister would like to have that part of the amendment in the bill. Surely these types of consideration should be equal to considerations of the economic environment.
Let me give another illustration. If a takeover by a foreign-owned food chain or other merchandising operation means the driving out of hundreds of Canadian small businessmen, corner groceries, small hardware merchants or clothiers, including some that are not so small, the takeover should not be allowed. That has to do with the social environment. By including the word "social" in the bill we would be saying that Canada in its own distinct way places great value on having a social environment that is distinct in nature. Small businesses then would not continually have the shirts ripped off their backs; they would not be swallowed up by the dozens, with those remaining gradually going belly-up. This situation has contributed to the vast destruction of rural Canada. For decades it has driven hundreds of small entrepreneurs out of this country. When is the minister going to wake up? Those are two reasons for inserting the words "politicsd and sociEd" in clause 2 of the bill.
Let me give a hypothetical example of what may happen if the amendment is not accepted. To a large extent the fertilizer industry is foreign-owned and controlled. There are a number of manufacturing plants in western Canada. The majority of them are foreign-owned and are controlled and directed from boardrooms in other countries. This industry is selling Canadian-made fertilizer packed in bags made in Canada, shipped on Canadian railway lines from Canadian fertilizer plants in Medicine Hat, Edmonton Eind Brandon to United States points where it is sold anywhere from $10 to $25 a ton less than it is sold to the farmer in Canada who lives beside the fertilizer plant.
Canadian farmers, individually and in groups, are trying to do something about their social and economic environment by banding together and ordering fertilizer at a point in either Montana or North Dakota. For example, a company in North Dakota assured a group of Canadian farmers delivery of 300 tons, six carloads, at $15 to $20 a ton less than they would pay in their own town. They received delivery of one car but the other five could not be delivered. That is very strange. I wish to cite another example. A farmer in Birch Hills, Saskatchewan, went to Montana, 450 miles away, and bought fertilizer for $20 a ton less than at home. This fertilizer had been

manufactured in Edmonton, only 200 miles from his home.
There will be further takeovers in the fertilizer industry. The minister needs our amendment so that he can call a halt to takeovers by international fertilizer companies. The minister should say to these firms that if they cannot guarantee they will sell these products at no higher price to Canadian consumers than they will sell to people across the line, a takeover will not be Eillowed. That has to do with the sociEil and politicsd environment as well as the economic environment; you cannot separate the three. The minister is diluting the situation by submitting that the economic environment is first in importance. I submit the three go hand in hand.
I hate to say this, Mr. Speaker, but some opposition members smd most members on the government side continue to contribute to the betrayal of our nationhood. Those are strong words. They contribute to this betrayal of our nation, albeit unwittingly and maybe even unwillingly, in ways which make one feel embarrassed and ashamed. This is probably the first time in history that Parliament has had a chance to do something about an issue of such magnitude and concern to Canadisms in all walks of life-but what do we get? We get this tiny, faltering, half-hearted step.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO CONTROL FOREIGN TAKEOVERS OF CANADIAN COMPANIES
speechtext: I do not want to sound like a flag-waver. In closing my remarks, I want to speak as sincerely as I can about our country and how we feel about it. We may not run Eiround waving flags, bragging and shooting off our mouths about it as much as people in other countries, but there is no question that this love is there. Surely it is not too much to ask the government of our country to do more than they are now prepared to do about our sovereignty and the control of our economic, social and political environment. We are a distinct country and a distinct people, geographically and socially. We have ways of doing things. We have a future that makes all Canadians, justifiably so, feel something special and that our country is special. I urge the minister to accept the amendment in order that we can give more weight to the last line in our anthem, "O Canada, we stand on guard for thee."

The hon. member over there asks what province is losing people. Big deal! I am not apologizing for that part of it. The hon. member who threw that question at me knows it was true in Alberta and it was also true in Manitoba. We were having difficulty. But we found in Saskatchewan, as in other provinces, that foreign ownership is beginning to encroach on our farmland, not because foreigners particularly want to farm our land because they think it is a good speculative proposition, but because it is a hedge. The provincial government became concerned. It brought in a bill to deal with the situation and that bill has been referred to a committee which will discuss it and decide what sort of legislation will finally be placed before the legislature to protect the land. What do we get from the other side of the House? Here is a headline in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix, "Ottawa opposes, Lang says". You have only one MP from the province of Saskatchewan.

speechtext:
Even before the bill becomes an act he intends, he says, to have it investigated. It is easy enough to say the matter will be hauled before the courts. Whether he will ever get round to it is something else. I doubt it. Hon. D. Steuart, leader of the opposition out there, is crying big crocodile tears; If you held out a dish you would be able to hear them splash. But as I say, some action is being taken.
In the city in which I live there was a refinery which was created by the people who work there. The refinery was started as a little highway refinery. Then it became BA, then it became Gulf. The decision was made to take it away. It is gone. It generated enough money to enable it to be placed there profitably. But at some point they decided it was to their advantage to place everything in the Edmonton area.
Foreign Takeovers Review Act
The Quaker Oats company decided it was to their advantage to locate their plant in Peterborough. They closed the other one down. They had no concern for the social implications of doing so. They had no consideration for anything except the prospect of making a buck. Maybe that is a good enough motivation for a company, but what kind of country would such a philosophy leave us? This question involves much more than ourselves; it involves generations who will come after us. Will they be able to play on the beaches of Prince Edward Island? Will they have access to the beaches of Ontario and Nova Scotia? What kind of country are we expecting? This is a valid question, I believe. It is more important in the long run than the question of how to make a buck most easily.
I read an article recently about the proposal to build a pipeline down the Mackenzie Valley. Answers to questions in the House indicate that a move of this kind is under way. But what about the effect on the ecology? This is a question which has not been answered. Apparently it is intended to go ahead anyway. But what about the people who live in the area? Don't they have rights? Do we have the right to set their wishes aside? Possibly we have the right legally-but morally? That is inevitable. Whether it concerns the Mackenzie Valley or the James Bay area, the decision will be made without very much consideration being given those who have managed to make a living satisfactory to them over a long period of time.
To get to the main substance of the bill and to the proposed amendments, surely the government must be aware of the very bad press this particular proposal has received. I have read hardly a newspaper article or editorial comment which says the bill is a good one, that the proposal is solid and will meet the needs of Canadians now and in the future.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR CONTROL OF FOREIGN OWNERSHIP OF CANADIAN COMPANIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 30 or 31 when I spoke in this debate I referred to the bill introduced by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) as an economic eunuch. I said that it amounted to a big zero and would not do anything at all to further the repatriation of Canada economically, culturally or socially. I realize the minister thinks that this is rather humorous. He is one of the more conservative and status-minded ministers of the government, which is very unfortunate since this is an issue about which Canadians are very concerned, as demonstrated by recent public opinion polls.
In many ways this issue has crossed party lines. The 13 mavericks in the Liberal party as well as some in the Conservative party, and the Committee for an Independent Canada, composed of all political stripes, are all concerned about foreign ownership in the Canadian economy. By no means does this bill go far enough to solve the economic independence of this country, which I suggest is what most rank and file members of the Canadian citizenry want at the present time. The bill deals only with

takeovers in the economy. As pointed out by the hon. member for Duvernay (Mr. Kierans), the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) and others, it relates to 5 per cent, 6 per cent or maybe 10 per cent of the total foreign ownership of this country.
For years there have been studies, task forces, commissions and public debates on the question of foreign ownership. We have had the Watkins report and the Gray report. In essence, both these major pieces of work, commissioned by Liberal governments, came to the same conclusion, namely, that the Canadian economy is far too much foreign-owned and controlled and that something must be done to repatriate it. Yet this is not being done.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR CONTROL OF FOREIGN OWNERSHIP OF CANADIAN COMPANIES
speechtext: Order, please. In pursuing his remarks along present lines, the hon. member seems to be debating the bill again on second reading. He is really debating the principles and objectives of the bill. I would invite the hon. member to bring his remarks to bear as closely as he can on the amendments before the House, which relate to the social and political effects of the bill.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR CONTROL OF FOREIGN OWNERSHIP OF CANADIAN COMPANIES
speechtext:
I agree with you, Mr. Speaker, and I have given the reason for our party moving several amendments. We have decided it is not a good bill. Because we are concerned about foreign ownership, we want to strengthen the bill. We are now debating the first amendment, moved by the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Salts-man), which deals with the social and political aspects of foreign ownership as well as the economic aspects. I think these aspects are very important.
The amendments which the minister is going to consider are not those that groups like the Committee for an Independent Canada and the members of our party would like to see moved. I suggest that instead of listening to his friends in the Canadian Manufacturers Association, the stock exchange, and so on, he should bear in mind the interests of the ordinary workers and farmers of Canada.
As already mentioned by others, the Ontario government announced during the last few weeks it will take action to ensure that more Canadians sit on the boards of companies in the province. The Saskatchewan government is preparing a bill dealing with the foreign ownership of farmland. These steps are very important to the political and social way of life of this country. They deal with problems that must be solved quickly if we are to have a united Canada that will forge ahead in future years.
Questions have been asked by members on the other side of the House, and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and others ask about our approach to foreign ownership. They ask, "What about your party going into foreign markets and getting money from Japan and the United States for development in Saskatchewan and Manitoba?" We have done that in some cases.
Let me give one example. When the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) was premier of Saskatchewan, our government went to the United States and borrowed hundreds of millions of dollars for the establishment of the Saskatchewan Power
June 26, 1972

Corporation. The one important thing was that this was loan capital, not equity capital. Now the people of the province of Saskatchewan own the Saskatchewan Power Corporation, rather than some United States industrialist living in Chicago, Detroit or elsewhere. This is a very important distinction and an important political choice which I hope the minister will realize and consider seriously.
History will show that nearly every country in the world has had to rely on foreign capital at some stage of its development. The classic example is the United States. During its development it had a great deal of money from the United Kingdom and other European countries. But it made sure that the majority of that money was loan capital and not equity capital. Now the people of the United States own their own economy.
The same thing has happened in countries such as Japan and Sweden. Some 30 or 35 years ago Sweden was primarily foreign owned and controlled. The Social Democratic Party which assumed power there in 1935 accomplished repatriation of the economy. That was a matter of top priority and an important political choice, one which this government should make. We in this country are prostituting our economic destiny to a greater extent than any other industrial country in the western world. I suggest this is an insult to Canadians and a tragic policy for this government.
There is a difference between loan capital and equity capital, and we should realize the difference. When you buy a house and pay off the mortgage in 25 or 35 years, you own the house; but in respect of the Canadian economy this is not the case. It is like inviting outsiders, whether Americans or Japanese, to come into our houses, make themselves at home, use the furniture and even take our wives, and we pay them to do so. We let them make their profits and go back home. This is what is happening in Canada. It is something our government must stop, but it must take a major political decision to stop it.
I suggest we finance many foreign takeovers in our country. A United States economist in the department of commerce stated in 1968 that about 94 per cent of the money invested in Canada by American corporations is Canadian money. Some 94 per cent of the funds invested is really Canadian money obtained on the Canadian financial market. Some is borrowed from Canadian banking and lending institutions and some is profit from existing foreign firms, reinvested in our economy. We are selling out our country with our own money. Again, the minister should realize this and make the positive political decision.
We have funds in this country and we have ability. If we had a government with guts and imagination, surely to God it could create some policies and legislation to put our economy in the hands of Canadians. How, precisely, can we do this? The answer has been outlined time and time again in the Watkins report, the Gray report, by the Commons Standing Committee on External Affairs, the Standing Committee on National Defence and by certain members of the Liberal party, the hon. member for Duvernay, the Canadian Labour Congress, and the NDP. We know how to do this. All we need now is a political
Foreign Takeovers Review Act
decision to repatriate our country. It could be done within a few years.
Another thing that concerns me about this bill is that not enough emphasis is placed on some of the political decisions which must be made, nor on some of the social and cultural aspects of the problem of foreign ownership of our economy. Four months ago I was speaking to a non-political group in Yorkton. Most of the people were not supporters of my party; they were young businessmen and executives. I was speaking about foreign ownership. During the question period one of the young people said there was something that might be even more important than economic control of our country being in the hands of foreign, multinational corporations. He suggested that the cultural and social influence the United States and other countries had on Canada was the most important thing.
In a few minutes this afternoon I want to try to underline that point. We have tended to ignore, eliminate or forget the powerful impact other countries can have on Canadian culture through the media, the theatre, the arts and such other things. Let me emphasize the importance to the minister and the government.
I remember back in the late 1950s when I was a student in elementary school in Saskatchewan. Many of us knew more about United States political figures than we knew about our own. We knew more about Abraham Lincoln, what he did and stood for, than we did about Sir John A. Macdonald; we knew more about Jefferson than we did about Laurier. This was in large part because many of the textbooks used in those schools were published in the United States. They were written by United States authors and contained American historical interpretations.
Perhaps the book publishing industry is an area that should receive high priority from this government. The government should look at it very closely from the point of view of assistance to make it truly Canadian. We should try to create a nation which has a special identity that is Canadian.
We have moved in some of these areas, and I do not condemn the government for absolutely everything it has done.
Three or four years ago the radio-television commission laid down guidelines and rules concerning broadcasting in this country. It said that within three years 80 per cent of radio and television stations must be Canadian-owned. We have pretty well attained that goal. This sort of thing can be done and must be done. It should be done in the book publishing industry, the film industry, the arts and such fields, as well as in economic areas in respect of resources, manufacturing, and so on. We should put more emphasis on these areas, then perhaps we would have a more vibrant country, that is more Canadian.
The French-speaking areas of this country have developed distinct culture that is Canadian. This is primarily so because they speak the French language and are less susceptible to the pressures of United States influence. I am very proud of that fact in Canada. I not only want to see it preserved, but stimulated. I should also like to see

June 26, 1972
Foreign Takeovers Review Act
this fact stimulated in respect of English-speaking Canadians. I think this is a very healthy thing.
Earlier the minister was questioned about the French language being the working language in Quebec. He was asked whether this should be a consideration when an outside company is considering a takeover in the province of Quebec. I suggest it should be a consideration because the working language of most people in Quebec is French. If a foreign corporation is to take over a Canadian corporation and ignore that fact, it should be a very serious consideration in government legislation. I am surprised that some of these things are not done, especially since the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce is from the province of Quebec and I am sure realizes it is a very important question in that part of Canada.
There are many other issues and points I would like to speak about, but my time is running out. However, I do want to emphasize that there are very important social and political considerations that we must take into account. Not all considerations in the country, when it comes to foreign ownership, are solely and distinctly economic. This country, for example, was built for many reasons other than economic. It did not make economic sense to build a nation that went east and west; all the natural economic and trade patterns went north and south but we went against some of these economic considerations.
My colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), outlined many of these aspects when he spoke earlier about lack of economic sense when the CPR and the CNR were established. However, we made this decision and it was a conscious political one. We wanted to build a nation that was distinctly different from the United States. I suggest that in the future we will have to make a great many decisions that are political rather than economic. They may be social and cultural rather than economic. These considerations should be embedded within a piece of legislation such as this. If they were, then perhaps this bill, which up to now is really a big nothing, would have at least some significance and would go a little way toward repatriating the Canadian economy, the Canadian society and the Canadian culture which I am sure all of us want to see developed.
Again I urge the minister to stop listening to the Canadian Manufacturers Association, to his friends in Bay Street and those in the stock exchange, and instead to listen to the ordinary Joes of this country, the ordinary people who are interested in building a Canada that will provide them with jobs and a future for their children. We all know that we export a great volume of raw materials and that this industry provides very few jobs. It is capital-intensive. We should make a conscious, political decision to put more emphasis on manufacturing industry that is labour-intensive. I refer the minister to his colleague, the hon. member for Duvernay. I am sure if the minister listened to him he could-

Mr. Speaker, I respect your remarks. It is rather difficult for some of us, because we are speaking on a subject that moves us very strongly and on a bill which apparently does not move the minister, to contain ourselves to the narrow restrictions of certain amendments. I urge the minister to accept this amendment. Canadians want changes in this area and I think it is the responsibility of the government to lead the way. subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR CONTROL OF FOREIGN OWNERSHIP OF CANADIAN COMPANIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in considering this matter I am reminded of the teacher who asked his class what was the capital of Canada and a pupil answered, "Mostly American". That is part of the problem that concerns us. We are considering the political and social impact of some of the economic factors which affect us. This makes me think of David Lloyd George of Great Britain when discussing a social problem of theirs. He said they were born paupers in the land of their birth. We are facing a somewhat similar situation in this country.
I would suggest to the minister and to the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Howard), who seems to be listening to the debate, that Canadians would like a piece of the action. This is really what we are talking about. We do not want all of it to be taken over by somebody else. If there is going to be a takeover here, we want to do it. This is what we are talking about. We would like a bill to help Canadians take over their own country. What concerns us is social, economic and political equality. In effect, we would like to walk around with some money in our jeans, in our own country, and we would like to feel that we have a stake in Canada.
The French have an expression "Maitres chez nous". I am sure the minister, while he might not recognize my accent, is familiar with the term. I am suggesting, Sir, that those who own or control a country have an interest in that country. What, then, are they going to do with it? This is the intent of the amendment.
As I have observed people generally, those who own a house or a business, or those who manage a business have an interest in it and want to promote it. Those who look at a corporation as something that somebody owns, such as an absentee landlord, do not have the same interest in promoting the equity of the corporation. They might if they had a sense of proprietorship in the corporation. Let
June 26, 1972

me give an example which is fairly close to me. I do not own a share in the Bell Telephone Company, but I have listened to the piles being driven for the new building down the street. Even in that sense I have a sense of proprietorship in it. At least I have suffered with them a little. It is a fine building which is serving a purpose here in Ottawa. I am trying to point out, Sir, that there are things in which we have an interest because we are Canadians.

speechtext:

He said: Mr. Speaker, I consider it an honour to be able to speak on a matter which, if it does not receive national acclaim today, certainly in the next few years will have to be faced by a government of Canada. The motion which appears today on the order paper is not put forward for the first time. It was introduced last year by the former hon. member for South Western Nova. It was reintroduced early this year in my name, went through the usual procedures and now we are able to debate it for the next hour.
The first thing I want to say is that the motion can be refined. It would be no trouble at all for any member of the House to look at this motion as it stands verbatim, to take it apart and destroy it. One or two of its phrases are highly unpopular. Had I taken the time earlier in the year to refine the motion further I might have changed certain phrases. The motion contains the phrase "a national conference on uniform standards in primary and secondary education". As an educator who has spent quite a number of years in classrooms, I take exception to anything that could be defined as a uniform standard for the classroom. No educator, no citizen would ever introduce a motion calling for a uniform standard to be applied to a classroom setting.
If I were to speak about a curriculum, not only do I believe that you cannot have a national curriculum but I believe you cannot even have a provincial curriculum or a
Federal-Provincial Relations
school curriculum in the standard sense. A curriculum is the total experience of an individual in the school or learning setting. It is something that exists at the individual level in the classroom. No educator would ever talk about a uniform standard applying to a curriculum process.
These are some points I want to clarify before hon. gentlemen opposite rise to speak on this motion. I would not consider uniform standards in terms of laying down in black and white what should transpire in an educational system across Canada in terms of text books, expenditures of funds or any of the specific goals of education. Again, these questions are not only of provincial nature but are better handled at the local level.
The purpose of this motion is to draw attention to the need for the federal government to recognize that in 1972 it has a responsibility in the area of human resource development, and to suggest that there should be a meeting of minds between municipalities, provinces, school boards, teachers and the national government to talk about all of the broader aspects of the educational process.
Turning back to 1867 when the nation of Canada was born, it is easy to understand that education was assumed to be a local issue. At that time it was totally a community issue. As a matter of fact, from studying the history of education in Canada we find that it was mainly the churches which became involved in the educational process. In those days very few people travelled from one part of the country to another. There was not the kind of mass migration that we see nowadays. And because of the political implications and realities of 1867, education was deemed to be purely a provincial issue.
For the last 25 or 30 years, broadminded educators have realized that education must be considered as something more than a provincial issue. The one thing that offends me even more as an educator than as a Member of Parliament is the hypocrisy of the various levels of government. Today the federal government is involved, actively and directly, in as many as 20 educational areas. But its hypocrisy is unbelievable. The federal government allocates funds to the provinces with which they can build vocational institutions. These facilities are owned by the provinces because of the constitutional hang-up. The provinces in turn sell seats in these institutions to the federal government, or rent space to the federal government, so that it can manage its federal manpower programs or adult occupation retraining programs. This avoids facing the reality of the situation, that vocational education is an integral part of the educational process and that there should be close liaison between the local educational systems at all levels, primary, secondary and post-secondary.
Again, Mr. Speaker, annually the federal government pays many millions of dollars to the provinces to be devoted to post-secondary education. The universities, which are an integral part of the educational process, receive their share of the federal revenue dollar but in effect never admit it. The provinces jealously guard what they consider to be a constitutional right. Recently a constitutional conference was held without a single aspect of education coming to the fore. I do not want to get involved in that debate, but when the provinces have a hang-up

June 26, 1972
Federal-Provincial Relations
over their constitutional and jurisdictional rights, and when the federal government maintains the hypocrisy of not wanting to get involved in education, it is the people of Canada who suffer the resultant hardship.
I do not have to tell my colleagues of the effect which the general mobility of the population has on our young people. All of us know of members of the armed forces who have been transferred around Canada, perhaps a dozen times in a decade, and know the effect this has had on the children involved. Each Member of Parliament who has brought his family to Ottawa can speak of the impact which lack of a common educational area has had on his family.
We are one of only two major countries in the western world which do not have a federal presence in their educational systems. I believe the federal government should face up to the fact that a major portion of the Canadian population is, or has been, in the process of moving from one part of Canada to another. Within the next decade perhaps all the population will move, once in a lifetime, from one part of Canada to another. This points to the need for the common presence of a national body in the area of education.
One of the biggest drawbacks to regional development is the lack of equal educational opportunities in the disadvantaged regions. Many provinces are fooling themselves whenever they stand up at a national conference and say they jealously guard their constitutional right over education. In effect they are denying their citizens equal educational opportunities. Unless we get the federal government involved in the educational process, the people of areas suffering regional disparity will continue to have a second-rate educational structure.
As examples I could mention several provinces but I will talk about my own because I know more about it. There is no way that my province can ever afford the share of the tax dollar that is necessary in order to provide its citizens with equal educational opportunities. We have not the tax revenues to provide the necessary school facilities. Here I am talking about the physical resource capability so that our young people may have the same opportunities as young people in Montreal or Toronto. Consequently, unless the provinces get off their high horses and the federal government is willing to involve itself directly in the educational process with the co-operation of the provinces, regional disparity will continue to exist.
As an example of how critical the situation is between the provinces and the federal government, all the regional development agreements are providing part of the infrastructure to certain areas for the building of schools. The federal government says it is part of the economic infrastructure. In Prince Edward Island some moneys have been allocated for school construction on the basis that the manpower capability will be needed in later years for economic development, so funds are allocated for education. What abominable hypocrisy that is, when we should be facing the reality that the province needs federal involvement-not direction but the type of involvement where physical and monetary resources are made avail-

able. Instead, the federal government, with the permission of the provinces, goes through about 20 back doors.
What I am saying, Mr. Speaker, is that in view of the fact that the federal government, with the co-operation of the provinces, is already involved in about 20 areas of educational development, in view of the fact that education today is more than a provincial and local issue, and in view of the mobility of the population, it is one of the imperatives of this Parliament that the federal government start talking to the provinces, the municipalities, the school boards and teachers to convene some sort of national conference on human resource development. It is almost out of order to use the word "education" in the House of Commons today, and indeed I am surprised that the Speaker has not ruled on that.
If there is to be a meeting of minds, we have to talk about an area of common interest and common involvement. We do not have to take authoritarian involvement or direction from Ottawa. We have to talk about the broad objectives of education which must be faced by the Canadian people. This is the intent of the motion. If we want some kind of equality of educational opportunity, if we want to eliminate the serious impact of the fragmentation of the process on the mobile public of the seventies, then we must start facing the facts.
Just before coming into the House today I spoke to some members of the armed forces and asked if they thought this motion had any relevance to their families. I was astounded to learn that the educational opportunities of many children had been ruined because when they moved from one system to another it was necessary to start the whole process over again.
As an educator, I could speak for hours on this subject and eliminate many of the arguments about uniform standards. That is not an adequate phrase and I could be blamed for not defining my motion. However, I hope that members taking part in the debate will not get hung up on that; I hope they will address their remarks to the question of some kind of common federal presence, and that they will be realistic enough to see that despite the fact it may be popular for members to stand at the end of the provincial road, they are also dealing with the lives of many thousands of Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject the hon. member has raised today is timely and is of general interest in this country. There is widespread interest in public education and, as he pointed out, Canada has become a nation of very mobile people. I believe that the average family moves something like once every five years, and undoubtedly many of those moves are across provincial boundaries.
The motion is pertinent, also, because we are all concerned about disparities which exist among certain geographical regions and among certain economic, social and cultural groups. I rather expected the hon. member to speak at some length on the need for uniform standards, but I agree with him that in Canada we should avoid rigid, uniform educational standards from coast to coast and from north to south. We are a country of variety and the
June 26, 1972

needs in one part of the country are not identical with the needs in another.
I, too, tend to believe that the curriculum should not be identical in the hon. member's riding with that in southern Ontario or my own riding in British Columbia. However, I must also say that more uniform standards than Eire presently available to our students would be desirable. All hon. members undoubtedly have examples.
I can recall a young high school student from British Columbia who was brought to Ottawa by her parents. Being the capital of the nation, where bilingualism is a policy, the pairents naturEilly expected that their daughter's knowledge of French would be furthered. It only took a short time for them to discover that the methods of teaching in British Columbia and Ontario were so different that if she were to pursue a French course here she would probably lose credits and possibly fail a year in school. As a result, the young lady took Spanish instead. This illustrates the need for some uniformity in education.
I think I should remind hon. members that there are considerable constitutional barriers to federal involvement in the field of education. The constitution clearly states that the power to legislate in the field of education belongs to the provinces, in and for each province. Most elementary and secondEiry education as well as postsecondary education is provided within the structures of the ten provincial systems. The federal government, naturally, must be concerned that all provinces have the resources necessEiry to provide at least a minimum service for Canadians, but its direct responsibility for elementary and secondary education is primarily limited to the Yukon and the Northwest Territories and, to some extent, to the native peoples. For post-secondary education it is confined specifically and constitutionally to the operation of our three military colleges.
Under these circumstances, I would suggest that the first initiative should come from the provinces; but I am not suggesting that the federal government has not been concerned with the way in which educational standards can be improved. A series of federal governments, Mr. Speaker, have shown active concern in various aspects of education-technical education, manpower training, higher education both in the universities and other types of post-secondary institutions, and the training of personnel for health and welfare services. The federal government for many years has been deeply involved in supporting university research programs.
The hon. member spoke at some length on the need for a federal presence in education in Canada. Mr. Speaker, we have a very considerable presence in education and I should like to put some figures on the record which are most significant in this respect. It is estimated that in the year 1960-61 the proportion of federal government support in relation to the total expenditures of all levels of government on education was 8.4 per cent; that is, of the 100 per cent contributed by provincial governments, municipal governments and the federal government, the federal government contributed 8.4 per cent. In the 197172 period the federal share had risen to 22.4 per cent. I might add that at present federal programs of education support sire under active review.
Federal-Provincial Relations
In my view, however, the body to which this motion ought to be addressed is the Council of Ministers of Education, established in 1967. The ministers of education of the ten provinces have somewhat slowly, but persistently developed a permanent structure with a central office in Toronto. Several federal cabinet ministers have on several occasions met with the council, as have federal officials with their council counterparts, on matters relating to our federal programs. Although these meetings will continue, I feel that the broader implications of this motion are such that the council itself should take whatever initiative it feels necessary.
I fully realize the seriousness of the differences and dispEirities which gave rise to the hon. member's request for a national conference. I am sure all members of this House are aware of unfortunate disparities across our land relating to the education of our children. I agree with the hon. member that there should be a greater federal presence in the area of education, but would remind him and the House that there is a considerable degree of federal presence in this area, inasmuch as more than one-fifth of the education money in Canada is being provided by the federal government. The provision of this money I feel is evidence of a most satisfying and significant presence.
I also agree that the federal presence is by no means sufficiently visible. If an initiative were to come from an interprovincial agency such as the Council of Ministers of Education, I am sure the federal government would be prepared to give its full co-operation and to continue its involvement in education for the good of the young people of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate because the motion moved by the hon. member from Newfoundland is of great importance. I agree with most of his statements and, speaking as an educator, share his concern regarding uniform standards of education across this country.
As we look at our process of education we must not forget that there is a certain flexibility as between one province and another in teaching methods. For example, in the field of social studies or history, the aspects students might study in Saskatchewan might be different from those they might study in Newfoundland. In Saskatchewan, a student studying history might be taken to the site of the Riel rebellion. Students in Newfoundland might not be able to do so.
On the other hand, since young people may move from one end of the country to the other, it is important to keep standEirds uniform. This affects, I think pEirticularly people of my generation and of the generation of the hon. member from Newfoundland who may be school teachers. People may train in one part of the country to be teachers, only to find that in time there might not be enough jobs for all those trained.
I submit that it is important for the federal government to introduce some kind of standard governing the employment of teachers in this country. If the federal government is lavishly to hand out, as has been suggested, 22.4 per cent of all money spent on education it ought, as the

June 26, 1972
Federal-Provincial Relations
hon. member from Newfoundland suggested, convene a national conference and deal with the problems of education on a national basis. We must remember that although the government pours money into technical and trade education, the people of this country are mobile. The young people of Saskatchewan may move to Toronto or Hamilton, and when they apply for a job in order to exercise their skills in the trade they have learned they may find themselves competing with 100, 200, 300 or 400 applicants from other parts of Canada who have taken the same kind of training on the assumption that jobs are available.
In this House we have taken part in interesting debates centering on the question of regional disparities. Regardless of anything the Council of Ministers of Education may say, I think it is up to the federal government to say whether we should introduce general standards in education which will meet the needs of our young people on a national scale as they become available for employment.
We must also consider the problem of young people who are trained in this country in a particular profession and who, not finding a job here, move to the United States in order to work in that profession. Only if there is a national program for providing employment in those sectors for which young people are being trained today will we be able to alleviate the problem of the exodus of our young, professional people to the United States. At the same time, of course, we must remember the social problems that arise from the mobility of our people. Relatives of mine in the armed forces have told me that young people moving from Noya Scotia to British Columbia, say, may encounter great difficulties in education. Also, apart from adjusting to the educational system, youngsters must make social and other adjustments.
We must also consider the difficulty, referred to by the parliamentary secretary, of financing education. When the British North America Act was passed in 1867 it was agreed that educational costs would be met by property taxes. It has become difficult to provide equal opportunities in education for all since property taxes are not sufficient for providing all the facilities required. The federal government, therefore, must come to grips with the question and determine whether the concept of financing education through property taxes-I am thinking of rural Saskatchewan in particular-is not outmoded and outdated. Is the property tax a large enough source of educational revenue in each of our provinces and municipalities?
The teaching profession at the post-secondary level in the last few years has developed some really interesting proposals for setting up a national council of educators which would look into the question of national standards. The parliamentary secretary told us of the Council of Ministers of Education. It is now incumbent on the federal government, I believe, to take such action as is suggested by the hon. member from Newfoundland and convene a national conference which will attempt to deal with the problems of education. I ought to deal with uniform standards as well as with the financing of education.
I conclude my remarks on this motion by expressing the hope that it will be voted on and will receive the unanimous support of the House. I compliment the hon.

member for bringing forward the motion and I commend its intent.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the private member's notice of motion No. 10, in the name of the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Lundrigan), reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government of Canada should consider the advisability of taking the initiative in securing the collaboration of the provinces in the convening of a national conference on uniform standards in primary and secondary education.
First, I want to congratulate the hon. member for bringing this question before the House. It is a matter of concern to many Canadians. A year or so ago, when I travelled with the constitutional committee to various parts of this country, it was a common complaint that when people move from one part of the country to another their children have to move back a grade or forward a grade in school. Often the subjects are not aligned so that this can be done in an easy way. Therefore, I am glad the hon. member has put this motion before the House today.
I am also glad that the hon. member is not talking about a uniform curriculum but about uniform standards. I suppose standards are the end result of work in a specific curriculum. That may pose some difficulty, but I am pleased that he does not want a uniform curriculum, which of course would be very difficult to achieve. I do not think anyone in this country would like to see one flat, monolithic curriculum across the country in which students from Bonavista to Vancouver Island would learn exactly the same thing on the same day.
The problem of curriculum is even greater than one might think. It was only four or five years ago that in the province of Ontario we had a greater level of uniformity across the province. There were provincial school inspectors who made sure that we had a standard across the province. Since then the province has been carved into 30 to 40 school divisions. These divisions have considerably more autonomy than the old, local township school area boards. We have a multiplicity of curricula and programs in our school system within the province of Ontario, let alone a diversity throughout the country. If there were uniform standards they would be of great advantage to the hundreds of thousands of people who move every year from one part of the country to another. A recent figure that I read suggested that one in four families moves every year. I do not know whether they move interprovin-cially or not.
The hon. member referred to the problem of regional disparity. He suggested that regional disparity somehow relates to education. I believe there is a link. If you look around the world you will find that a reasonably high level of education and training-I use that term advisedly because surely training for a specific job is almost as important as broad, general academic education-well distributed throughout the population is probably the greatest factor in determining the relative affluence of any country. In many countries with tremendous capital investment, the average individual is poor. Many countries are very rich in natural resources but the people are relatively poor. In several countries, people with a high
June 26, 1972

level of education and training are not generally distributed throughout the population and there is a very low standard of living.
The hon. member made a good point when talking about regional development, but I am not sure that establishing standards across the board is essential. If we suggested that to the minister of education for Newfoundland, he might be inclined to look at us as federal people who are trying to stick our noses into the provincial pot. He might say something like Sir Winston Churchill said to the North American continent in the dark days of World War II: Give us the tools and we'll finish the job.
I think we can attack the problem of regional disparity, without setting uniform standards, by providing extra funds. The federal government has provided a great deal of funds to Newfoundland. I understand that through the special areas program, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has made funds available for school construction. The federal government is putting a great deal of money into education in every province of this country.
I recently noticed a question on the order paper concerning grade 13 education in the province of Ontario, whether grade 13 was considered to be university level for the purpose of federal assistance. We found out that it is. In fact, 50 per cent of the eligible operating expenditures as defined in the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act, 1967, for grade 13 education in the province of Ontario are borne by the federal government. This is not generally known in the province. The provincial government probably does not mention this any more than necessary.
In the answer to this question on the order paper I read that in the fiscal year 1967-68, $16 million was provided for grade 13 education, and for the fiscal year 1971-72 it is estimated that almost $33 million will be provided by the federal government to the province of Ontario for the educational costs of grade 13. I think we can see from these figures that the federal government is deeply involved in education both at the university level and, at least in the province of Ontario, at the grade 13 level.
The real problem in the motion before us this afternoon is a constitutional one. Section 93 of the British North America Act makes it quite clear that education is primarily a matter of provincial responsibility. There have been many incidents throughout history where the provinces have made it quite clear that although they will accept money from the federal government for education, they do not want to hand over any of the responsibility for education to the federal government.
I might mention some of the areas in which the federal government is involved in education. Perhaps the newest is the bilingualism program under which funds are made available to provincial departments of education. A group from one of the high schools in my constituency recently asked me whether funds could be made available for a special immersion course. The response from the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) was that funds are already available to provincial governments for such training, so it was impossible to get federal funds directly. Federal
Federal-Provincial Relations
funds are also available in connection with the retraining and upgrading program. This is really a most important form of education because we are training men and women to do the jobs which are available for them.
The federal government is also deeply involved in the education of Indians and Eskimos. I understand that even here there is a great deal of diversity in programming, in the elementary schools at least. I do not know whether there are separate high schools on Indian reserves but the levels adopted in each province are the levels adopted by the schools for which the federal government is responsible as far as the curriculum of each is concerned. Criticism has been expressed in some provinces in connection with the role of the federal government in education through television. We read recently that the minister of transport of Quebec and the responsible provincial minister in Ontario were seeking increased jurisdiction over television and cablevision within their provincial boundaries. This is one area, I suppose, in which there will continue to be constitutional argument.
I was interested in the statement by the parliamentary secretary that between the fiscal year 1960-1961 and the fiscal year 1970-1971 the percentage of the cost of education borne nationally had risen from 8.4 to 24.4. I mentioned earlier that the committee on the constitution during its hearings throughout the country often heard it argued that there was a need for national standards in education. In this connection, it was interesting to read what is contained in the committee's report. The committee studied this subject and deals with it in recommendation No. 88. It reads:
Education as such should remain exclusively a provincial power as it is at present subject to the guarantee for minorities set out elsewhere in this report.
Recommendation 89 reads:
The provinces should create a permanent office for co-operation and co-ordination in education and federal participation should be confined to the area of federal jurisdiction over the education of native peoples, immigrants, defence oersonnel and dependants.
So, the committee seems to have opted for the idea of diversity. The permanent office has since been established, I understand, by the Council of Ministers of Education.
It seems to me that what is being proposed is a national conference. If such a conference were not sponsored by the ministers of education, it is likely that no provincial representatives would attend. So it appears that if we are to have a conference of the type suggested, it should really be sponsored by the Council on Education. Even if it were to do so, I do not know whether a national conference is really the place at which to hammer out guidelines toward a national standard system. Young people and educators tell me, when I talk to them, that many students are already placed in different grades for different subjects. Thus, for example, a child could be in grade eight as far as his class report is concerned, but he could be in grade four for reading and grade seven for mathematics. With an open approach of this kind, implying far greater elasticity in the school timetable, it would surely be even more difficult to create uniform standards for each grade and to do so would require all the ingenuity of our educators.

The hon. member appears to be concerned. I do not know why. While he was speaking he appeared to be apologizing for his motion, anticipating there would be criticism of his idea. I realize his motion deals not with the curriculum, but with standards. But surely, in the end, standards are reflected in the curriculum. Yet I understand the hon. member's difficulty. We want a system which is flexible, one which gives a person a broad education so that he can enjoy life while still providing substantial training as a basis for a future occupation. We hear about students in Ottawa who have already taken a BA degree and who then attend Algonquin College to acquire specific training.
What I am saying, in effect, is that although the hon. member's objectives are perhaps laudable we are a long way from realizing them, partly because the sort of education system he seems to have in mind is already ceasing to exist; more emphasis is placed on individual training and there is more training of the individual for a specific job.
